title: Edges in a tree
question: A connected tree has 12 nodes and no cycles. How many edges does it have?
options: 12, because every node owns exactly one outgoing edge to its parent or child
11, because every node except the root is attached by exactly one edge
13, because a connected structure needs one extra edge to close the root
6, because each edge links a pair of nodes and so covers two of them
explanation: In a tree every node except the root hangs from exactly one parent edge, so n nodes give n - 1 edges. The root has no parent edge, which rules out n. Adding an edge beyond n - 1 would create a cycle, and halving the count ignores that edges are shared only at the endpoints, not consumed.

title: Height of a tree
question: A tree consists of a single root node with no children. Using the common convention of counting edges, what is its height?
options: 1, because the tree contains one node and that node sits on level one
Undefined, because height only makes sense once a tree has at least one edge
0, because the longest path from the root to a leaf has no edges
2, because the root counts once as a parent and once as a leaf
explanation: Height is the number of edges on the longest path from the root down to a leaf, and a lone root is itself a leaf, so that path has zero edges. Counting nodes instead of edges would give 1, which is a different convention (often called depth in levels). The case is well defined, and the root is counted only once.

title: Post-order traversal use
question: Which traversal visits both children of a node before the node itself, making it the natural order for freeing every node of a tree safely?
options: Pre-order, which handles the node first so the parent link is cleared before children
In-order, which handles the left child, then the node, then the right child
Level-order, which handles all nodes of one depth before going deeper
Post-order, which handles the left subtree, the right subtree, then the node
explanation: Post-order processes the children first and the parent last, so a node is only released after everything below it is gone. Pre-order would release a parent first and lose the references to its children, in-order frees the node in the middle of its two subtrees, and level-order frees shallow nodes before deeper ones that still hang from them.

title: What a leaf is
question: In a rooted tree, what makes a node a leaf?
options: It has no children, so no edge leads downward from it
It sits on the deepest level, regardless of how many children it has
It is the only node without a parent, so the traversal begins there
It has exactly one child, so it ends a chain of single links
explanation: A leaf is simply a node with no children. A node on the deepest level is always a leaf, but leaves can also appear on shallower levels, so depth does not define them. The node without a parent is the root, and a node with one child is an internal node, not a leaf.

title: In-order visiting sequence
question: For a binary tree, which sequence describes an in-order traversal of the subtree rooted at a node?
options: Visit the node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree
Visit the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node
Visit the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree
Visit the right subtree, then the node, then the left subtree
explanation: In-order places the node between its two subtrees: left subtree, node, right subtree. Node first is pre-order, node last is post-order, and visiting the right subtree before the left is the mirrored (reverse in-order) variant that yields the reverse sequence.

title: Max-heap property
question: What does the max-heap property guarantee about a node and its children?
options: Every node is at least as large as each of its children, with no order between siblings
Every node is larger than its left child and smaller than its right child
The values are fully sorted when read level by level from top to bottom
Every node is at least as large as every value stored on the same level
explanation: The max-heap property only relates a parent to its children: the parent is greater than or equal to each child, and siblings are in no particular order. Ordering left against right is the binary search tree rule, a full level-by-level sort is stronger than a heap provides, and values on one level are not compared with each other.

title: Inserting into a min-heap
question: How does a min-heap insert a new value while keeping its shape and ordering?
options: Put it at the root and push the old root down until the order is restored
Place it in the next free slot at the bottom, then swap it upward while it is smaller than its parent
Walk down from the root to the correct sorted position and shift later values aside
Append it at the end of the array and re-sort the whole array afterwards
explanation: The new value goes into the first free position of the last level, which keeps the tree complete, and is then swapped with its parent while it is smaller, a step called sift-up. It moves along one root-to-leaf path, so insertion costs O(log n). Starting at the root, shifting a sorted sequence, or re-sorting everything all do more work than needed.

title: Largest value in a min-heap
question: A min-heap holds n distinct numbers. What is the cost of finding the largest one when you only have the heap operations?
options: O(n), because the maximum can be any leaf and none of them is marked
O(1), because the maximum always sits at the last position of the array
O(log n), because it lies along the path from the root to the leftmost leaf
O(1), because the root keeps both the smallest and the largest values
explanation: A min-heap only orders each parent against its children, so the maximum must be one of the leaves, and there is no rule saying which. You have to inspect about half of the elements, which is O(n). The last array position is not guaranteed to hold it, the leftmost path is not special, and the root stores only the minimum.

title: Removing the root of a heap
question: After the root of a max-heap is removed, which repair step restores a valid heap?
options: Shift every remaining value one position toward the front of the array
Promote the larger of the root's two subtrees by rotating the tree
Move the last element to the root and sift it down, swapping with its larger child
Rebuild the heap by inserting all remaining values again one by one
explanation: Moving the last element into the root keeps the tree complete, and sifting it down, always swapping with the larger child, restores the order in O(log n). Shifting the array breaks the parent-child index rules, rotations belong to balanced search trees, and reinserting every value costs O(n log n) for no benefit.

title: Heap versus search tree ordering
question: Why is a heap a poor choice for printing all values in sorted order without extra work, compared with a binary search tree?
options: A heap keeps its values in a linked structure, so it cannot be traversed efficiently
A heap orders only parents against children, so reading it in order does not give sorted output
A heap cannot hold duplicate values, so the sorted output would lose entries
A heap is rebuilt on every read, which makes any sorted listing too slow
explanation: A heap guarantees only that each parent beats its children, so an in-order or level-order read gives no overall order, whereas an in-order walk of a binary search tree is sorted. Heaps are commonly stored in arrays, accept duplicates, and are not rebuilt on reads. To get sorted output you repeatedly extract the root, which is heap sort.

title: Searching a binary search tree
question: While searching for the key 40 in a binary search tree, you reach a node holding 55. What should you do next?
options: Stop and report that the key is absent, since 55 is already larger than 40
Continue in the right subtree, because keys larger than the node are stored there
Check both subtrees, since the key could be on either side of 55
Continue in the left subtree, because 40 is smaller than 55
explanation: A binary search tree keeps smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right, so 40 compared with 55 sends the search left. Stopping would be wrong because 40 can still exist in the left subtree. Going right only suits larger keys, and checking both sides gives up the pruning that makes the search fast.

title: Finding the maximum in a BST
question: Where is the largest key of a non-empty binary search tree located?
options: At the node reached by following right children from the root until none remains
At the root, since it is the ancestor of every other key in the tree
At the leftmost leaf, reached by following left children from the root
At the deepest leaf, which is always the last key that was inserted
explanation: Larger keys always go right, so repeatedly following right children ends at the maximum, which has no right child. The root is only the largest when it has no right subtree. The leftmost node holds the minimum, and the deepest leaf depends on insertion history rather than key size.

title: The search tree invariant
question: Which statement correctly defines the ordering rule of a binary search tree?
options: Each node is larger than its left child and smaller than its right child, and nothing more
For every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller and all in its right subtree are larger
The keys increase along every path from the root down to a leaf
Each level holds larger keys than the level above it, from the root downward
explanation: The rule applies to whole subtrees, not just direct children: every key on the left is smaller than the node and every key on the right is larger. A child-only comparison would let a deep node violate the order, keys need not rise along every path since left children are smaller, and levels are not globally ordered.

title: Directed versus undirected edges
question: In a social network where following someone does not oblige them to follow back, which graph model fits best?
options: An undirected graph, because every edge connects exactly two people
A complete graph, because any two people could in principle follow each other
A directed graph, because each edge has a source and a target
A weighted tree, because every account has a single parent account
explanation: A follow relationship has a direction, so it is modelled by a directed edge from the follower to the followed account. An undirected edge would force the relation to be mutual. A complete graph describes a network where all pairs are linked, and a tree would forbid cycles and multiple followers per account.

title: Sum of degrees
question: An undirected graph has 15 edges. What is the sum of the degrees of all its vertices?
options: 15, because each edge is counted once at the vertex where it starts
225, because every vertex can be connected to as many as 15 others
It cannot be known, because the vertex count is needed to compute it
30, because each edge adds one to the degree of both endpoints
explanation: Each undirected edge touches two vertices, so it contributes 1 to each endpoint's degree and 2 to the total, giving 2 x 15 = 30. Counting once ignores the second endpoint, squaring the edge count is meaningless here, and the vertex count is not needed because the total depends only on the number of edges.

title: Depth-first search bookkeeping
question: Which structure lets a depth-first search of a graph remember where to backtrack, whether made explicit or through recursion?
options: A stack, because the most recently discovered vertex is explored first
A queue, because the earliest discovered vertex is explored first
A min-heap, because the vertex with the smallest label is explored first
A hash set alone, because it records which vertices were already seen
explanation: Depth-first search follows one path as deep as possible and then backs up to the most recent branching point, which is last-in first-out behaviour, so a stack (or the call stack) fits. A queue produces breadth-first order, a heap would order by priority, and a visited set prevents repeats but cannot say where to return.

title: The root of a trie
question: In a trie that stores words letter by letter, what does the root node represent?
options: The first letter shared by all stored words, which is always stored at the root
The empty prefix, with one outgoing edge for each possible first letter
The longest word stored, since every other word is a prefix of it
The most recently inserted word, so that repeated lookups are faster
explanation: A trie spells words along paths, so the root stands for the empty prefix and its children correspond to the possible first letters. Words need not share a first letter, the longest word is a leaf rather than the root, and the trie keeps no record of insertion order.

title: Listing trie words alphabetically
question: How can all words stored in a trie be listed in alphabetical order without any separate sorting step?
options: Collect every word first and then run a comparison sort on the resulting list
Insert the words into the trie again, this time in reverse alphabetical order
Walk the trie depth first, visiting each node's children in letter order
Read the nodes level by level, since shorter words always sort before longer ones
explanation: Because each node's children are keyed by letter, a depth-first walk that visits children in alphabetical order emits the words in dictionary order, with no extra sort. Sorting afterwards is unnecessary work, reinserting does not change the structure, and level order lists short words first even when they sort later, such as zoo before apple.

title: What find returns
question: In a disjoint-set (union-find) structure, what does the find operation return for an element?
options: The representative of the set that currently contains the element
A list of every other element that belongs to the same set
The number of elements that are in the same set as the element
The element that was merged into the set most recently
explanation: Find returns a representative, usually the root of the element's tree, and two elements are in the same set exactly when their representatives are equal. It does not enumerate the members, it does not return the set size unless that is stored separately, and it does not track merge history.

title: Shape of a matrix product
question: Matrix A has 3 rows and 4 columns, and matrix B has 4 rows and 5 columns. What shape does the product A times B have?
options: 4 rows and 4 columns, since the shared dimension becomes the new size
3 rows and 4 columns, because the product keeps the shape of the first matrix
5 rows and 3 columns, because the dimensions are swapped by the product
3 rows and 5 columns, taking the outer dimensions of the two matrices
explanation: Multiplication requires the inner dimensions to match (4 and 4) and they disappear, leaving the rows of A and the columns of B, so the result is 3 by 5. The shared dimension does not become a size, the shape of A is not preserved when B has a different column count, and swapping dimensions describes a transpose, not a product.
